People these days feel like the only solid conclusion to a character's arc is to kill them off. Personally, I disagree; killing a character is usually lazy storytelling unless it has some significance to their development. For example, a coward sacrificing himself to save his friends or a villain dying because of their arrogance can add depth to the narrative.

I understand your perspective; if there's no real danger for the characters, it can feel pointless. 

However, what I'm suggesting is that killing off a character to conclude their arc has become a frequent trope in storytelling, and often it feels like a missed opportunity. This is especially true for villain characters. Many narratives wrap up with "we defeated the main antagonist and their followers, and now everything is perfect."

Consider how certain animated series handle their antagonists. They provide excellent examples of not simply eliminating the main villains, often allowing them to play significant roles in subsequent episodes. These characters might join the protagonists, face imprisonment while reflecting on their actions, or even undergo personal growth and change.

To me, this approach leads to more engaging storytelling. The villains aren't just one-dimensional; they are individuals with their own viewpoints.

That said, everyone I know claims I have too much empathy for antagonists. /shrug

I won't go into too much detail because I can't explain it very eloquently. The US also relied on "body count" as a measure of success in military operations. Soldiers could never find the local fighters, so they could never accumulate the numbers. Oh man, this reminds me of the time my high school principal accused me of being a potential school shooter because of an assignment for a writing class that I left in another classroom.

In writing class, we were doing obituaries and could choose to write them about a classmate or a generic person from a short story we read.

I chose my friend. I wrote it up and drew a little doodle of his funeral with "RIP" written on it.

Later, I attended a one-time guest speaker presentation in another class and continued to doodle the whole time. But when I left, I forgot my notebook with all of this in it on the table.

Later in the day, my friend gets called into the office because his name is in the notebook. Then I get called to the office when he tells them it's mine.

The principal proceeds to give me a big lecture on how everything in my notebook is unacceptable and is the EXACT SAME kind of stuff they found in the notebooks of infamous school shooters, specifically writing someone's obituary. I explain to her that the content she is upset about was a class assignment, and then she gets all confused and flustered before ordering me to never draw at school again. I'm like, "Sure, whatever, can I go now?"

I told all my friends about it later, and one of them, who fancied themselves a student activist, told me that was unfair and apparently went to her office to confront her on my behalf, but I never heard anything else about it.

A small town with fewer than 300 students in the school. Most of the faculty were either genuinely good people or those who abused their authority. I could write a short book on the strange or nonsensical events that occurred on a daily basis.

That's not how you do it, my friend.
